--- title: "Jump Analysis in R - Part 2: Creating an Interactive Plot" description: "In part two of this series, we will make the plot interactive, allowing the user to see all of the values being plotted" author: - name: Andrew Kates url: https://github.com/AKates717 date: 05-01-2025 categories: ["S&C","R", "ggplot2"] image: CMJ1.png # format: # html: # fig-width: 4 # fig-height: 3 draft: false execute: echo: true code-fold: show code-tools: true editor_options: chunk_output_type: console reference-location: document toc-location: left code-annotations: hover filters: - line-highlight --- In [Part One](https://andrewkates.netlify.app/Posts/2024-08-19-cmj-tracking1/) of this series, we created a plot to visualize Countermovement jump (CMJ) heights for one athlete across five testing dates. ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The static plot created in Part 1 of this series.](index_files/figure-html/fig-cmj0-1.png){#fig-cmj0 width=672} ::: ::: To briefly recap, this plot shows daily average, daily maximum, and each individual jump height, along with the average across all five days. Although I am happy with the style of the plot, and the amount of information I have been able to include, there is one major flaw with the final product: we have not communicated any actual values to our audience. Picture it, you share your beautiful plot with a coach or athlete and their first question is: "How high did I jump?". If all you have is this plot, what are you going to tell them? ![](images/jason%20segel%20idk%20GIF.gif){fig-align="center"} In this post, I will show you how to use `plotly` to make our plot interactive, allowing us to convey this vital information to our audience without compromising the minimalist aesthetic of the plot. We will accomplish this in two steps: 1. **Create an interactive plot (EASY):** In this section I will walk through some steps to get set up, then I will share the two lines of code needed to easily convert our `ggplot2` to a `plotly` plot. 2. **Customizations for `plotly` (ADVANCED):** In this section I will share some advanced `plotly` options which will allow us to produce a professional looking plot that you can be proud to share with coaches and athletes. # 1. Creating an Interactive Plot ## 1a. Getting Set Up If you are starting from scratch and do not have all the data loaded from the [previous](https://andrewkates.netlify.app/Posts/2024-08-19-cmj-tracking1/ "Part 1") post, you will need to download the jump data file [here](https://github.com/AKates717/my-website/blob/master/recent_five.csv). You will then need to open and copy the code below into your R environment. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} library(tidyverse) library(vroom) library(janitor) recent_five <- vroom("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AKates717/my-website/refs/heads/master/recent_five.csv") ak_plot_theme <- function(..., base_size = 12) { theme( text = element_text(size = base_size), axis.ticks = element_blank(), axis.title = element_text(color = "black", face = "bold"), axis.text = element_text(color = "black", face = "bold"), axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, hjust =0.6, vjust = 0.8), plot.title.position = "plot", plot.title = element_text(size = 16, color = "black", vjust = 5), plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "black", hjust = 0.5), plot.caption = element_text(size = 8, face = "italic", color = "black"), panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#e0e0e0"), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#ffffff"), plot.background = element_blank(), panel.border = element_blank()) } #draw a line between the mean and the max jump height mean_peak <- function(x) { data.frame(y = (mean(x) + 0.0001), ymax = max(x), ymin = mean(x)) } ``` ::: At this point, if all the code from the previous post has been loaded, you will be able to re-create the plot by running the following: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} recent_five %>% ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T))) + stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") + stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") + stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov), fun.data=mean_peak, geom="pointrange", size = 2, colour = "#D19A2B") + stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = 5), fun = "mean", geom = "line", linewidth = 1, colour = "#D19A2B") + geom_jitter(aes(y = flight_height_tov), shape = 1, size = 4, alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2) + geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean(flight_height_tov)), alpha = 0.3, linetype = 2, linewidth = 3) + ak_plot_theme() + labs( x = NULL, y = "Jump Height (cm)", title = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Once again, the static plot.](index_files/figure-html/fig-cmj1-1.png){#fig-cmj1 width=672} ::: ::: Now that we have our static plot, we can complete two additional set-up tasks. Firstly, go ahead and load the `plotly` package (you may have to install it first). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(plotly) ``` ::: Secondly, we will do a bit of data wrangling to add a nicely formatted date column into the `recent_five` dataframe. These dates will be added into the plot later in this post, and will help improve the readability of the ***tooltips***[^1]. [^1]: "Tooltips" are the labels that appear when you hover your cursor over the plotted data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} recent_five <- recent_five %>% mutate(date_mmmddyear = format(Date, "%b %d, %Y")) #<1> ``` ::: 1. `"%b %d, %Y"` will return the format mmm dd, yyyy, e.g. May 1, 2025 which I find much more intuitive to read at a glance, compared to 2025-05-01. ## 1b. Create a `ggplotly` This part is very simple. We take the code used to generate the static plot and save it as an object using `plot <-`, then we use a new function called `ggplotly` which returns the new interactive plot. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot <- recent_five %>% #<< ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T))) + stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") + stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") + stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov), fun.data=mean_peak, geom="pointrange", size = 2, colour = "#D19A2B") + stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = 5), fun = "mean", geom = "line", linewidth = 1, colour = "#D19A2B") + geom_jitter(aes(y = flight_height_tov), shape = 1, size = 4, alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2) + geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean(flight_height_tov)), alpha = 0.3, linetype = 2, linewidth = 3) + ak_plot_theme() + labs( x = NULL, y = "Jump Height (cm)", title = NULL) ggplotly(plot) #<< ``` ::: {#fig-cmj2 .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` An interactive plot ::: ::: Now when you hover your cursor over any of the data, you will see a ***tooltip*** pop-up showing the data associated with that plot point. You will also notice a ***modebar*** in the top right-hand corner of the plot, offering options such as the ability to zoom in/out, or to select different areas of the plot. Go ahead and play around with all of these new features before moving on to the next section. # 2. Advanced Upgrades for `Plotly` We now have an interactive plot which displays our data nicely, and also allows you and your audience to view exact jump heights. In my opinion, however, we can still improve the quality of the plot and make it look more professional by applying some custom formatting, particular by targeting the ***tooltips*** and the ***modebar***. ## 2a. Improve the "Tooltips" There's a lot of new things going on in this code block. You can read more about each change by hovering over the numbered annotations to the far right of each updated line of code. Hopefully this gives you a good idea of how each new line has contributed to the new plot seen below. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot <- recent_five %>% ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T), text = date_mmmddyear)) + #<1> stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") + stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") + stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov), fun.data=mean_peak, geom="pointrange", size = 2, colour = "#D19A2B") + stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = 5), fun = "mean", geom = "line", linewidth = 1, colour = "#D19A2B") + geom_jitter(aes(y = flight_height_tov), shape = 1, size = 4, alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2) + geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean(flight_height_tov)), alpha = 0.3, linetype = 2, linewidth = 3) + ak_plot_theme() + labs( x = NULL, y = "Jump Height (cm)", title = NULL) ggplotly(plot, tooltip = "text") %>% #<2> style(hovertemplate = "%{text}
Mean: %{y}", traces = 1) %>% #<3> style(text = paste(recent_five$Jump, "\n", recent_five$flight_height_tov), traces = 4) %>% #<4> style(text = paste("Five Day Average:",mean(recent_five$flight_height_tov) %>% round(2)), traces = 5) %>% #<5> style(hoverinfo = "skip", traces = c(2,3)) #<6> ``` ::: {#fig-cmj3 .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Improving the tooltips ::: ::: 1. Here, I've added a new aesthetic to the plot: `text = date_mmmddyear`. This is the nicely formatted date that was created above, and makes it easier to see the exact date. 2. Here, I've added `tooltip = "text"` as an argument in `ggplotly`. If I stopped coding here, every point on the plot would be labelled with only the date. The rest of the labels will be added below with more custom formatting. 3. "Trace 1" refers to the large gold points displaying mean jump height. I am using some html to display the date in **bold**, and the jump height on a new line with the heading *Mean:* in *italics.* 4. "Trace 4" is the `geom_jitter` that displays each individual jump. I want this tool tip to display the data in the "Jump" column on one line (i.e. Jump 1, Jump 2, etc) and the jump height on a second line. 5. "Trace 5" is the `geom_hline` showing the average jump performance across all five days. I've used some html and the `round()` function to make this look nice. 6. I want to "skip" the labels on traces 2 (max jump height) and 3 (the line connecting mean and max) because these labels are redundant. ## 2b. Improve the "Modebar" This is a minor upgrade that can easily be skipped, but I generally like to keep my plots as clean as possible, and there are some options in the ***modebar*** that will not be necessary. The first new line of code removes the plotly logo, and the second line removes all of the ***modebar*** options that we will not be needing. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot <- recent_five %>% ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T), text = date_mmmddyear)) + stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") + stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") + stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov), fun.data=mean_peak, geom="pointrange", size = 2, colour = "#D19A2B") + stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = 5), fun = "mean", geom = "line", linewidth = 1, colour = "#D19A2B") + geom_jitter(aes(y = flight_height_tov), shape = 1, size = 4, alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2) + geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean(flight_height_tov)), alpha = 0.3, linetype = 2, linewidth = 3) + ak_plot_theme() + labs( x = NULL, y = "Jump Height (cm)", title = NULL) ggplotly(plot, tooltip = "text") %>% style(hovertemplate = "%{text}
Mean: %{y}", traces = 1) %>% style(text = paste(recent_five$Jump, "\n", recent_five$flight_height_tov), traces = 4) %>% style(text = paste("Five Day Average:",mean(recent_five$flight_height_tov) %>% round(2)), traces = 5) %>% style(hoverinfo = "skip", traces = c(2,3)) %>% config(displaylogo = FALSE) %>% #<< config(modeBarButtonsToRemove = c("hoverCompare", "hoverclosest", "zoomIn2d", "zoomOut2d", "lasso2d")) #<< ``` ::: {#fig-cmj4 .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Cleaning up the Modebar ::: ::: ## Before and After By viewing the standard `ggplotly` side-by-side with the upgraded plot, and interacting with each one, you can see how these changes have greatly improved the readability of the plot. ::: {#fig-cmj5 .cell layout-ncol="2"} ::: {#fig-cmj5-1 .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Standard ggplotly ::: ::: {#fig-cmj5-2 .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Upgraded ggplotly, nicely formatted ::: A comparison to highlight the improvements we've made to a standard ggplotly. ::: # Next Steps In this blog post I have provided code to produce an interactive plot which can be used to compare CMJ performance over time, while also allowing the user to observe exact jump height values. In part 3 of this series I will walk through one method of adding some data analysis to the plot, in order to visualize real changes in jump performance that might indicate changes in neuromuscular status. Thanks for reading! This post is part of a short series. You can find the other posts linked below: - [Part 1: Jump Analysis in R - Visualizing Individual Performance](https://andrewkates.netlify.app/Posts/2024-08-19-cmj-tracking1/ "Part 1") - (Coming Soon) Part 3: Adding data analysis to our plots to measure changes in jump performance
